extracted.intended_audience: editors, copyeditors, writers, and publishers who apply Chicago Manual of Style capitalization rules
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and guidance for capitalizing personal names, titles, honorifics, places, organizations, and words derived from proper names according to the Chicago Manual of Style conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic titles and offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize formal academic titles used as part of a name or as honorifics (e.g., Professor Payne; Dean Boyer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Mark Payne, chair of the Department of Classics; Professor Payne; John W. Boyer, dean of the College'. See also specific rules (8.30) for variations when titles follow a name or are used generically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Named professorships
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize named professorship titles when used as official titles in conjunction with a name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Wendy Doniger, Mircea Eliade Distinguished Service Professor of the History of Religions in the Divinity School; Professor Doniger; Anthony Grafton, Dodge Professor of History, Princeton University; Professor Grafton.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Professor emeritus/emerita forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the gendered forms emeritus/emerita and their plurals as honorary designations and capitalize when used as part of a formal title (e.g., Professor Emerita Neugarten).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that emeritus/emerita are honorary designations and not simply 'retired'. Provide masculine/feminine/plural forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student-status terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Lowercase terms denoting student status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'freshman or first-year student, sophomore, junior, senior.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of degrees and fellowships (generic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lowercase names of degrees, fellowships, and similar when referred to generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a master’s degree; a doctorate; a fellowship; master of business administration (MBA).' Use capitalization for formal degree names when appropriate per other rules (see 10.21).

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive titles in apposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic descriptive titles (occupation/role) preceding a name are lowercased and treated as if in apposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the historian William McNeill (not Historian McNeill)'. See 8.21 and compare to 8.28.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic and academic honors after a name
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles denoting civic or academic honors when following a personal name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Roberta Bondar, Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada; the fellows.' For awards/abbreviations see related sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles of nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally capitalize titles of nobility (they form an integral part of a person’s name); lowercase the generic element (duke, earl, etc.) when used alone as a short form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Prince Charles; the prince; the Duke and Duchess of Windsor; the duke; the marquess; Lord Bath.' Note British usage subtleties (royal dukes) and consult specialized references for complex cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honorifics and respectful forms of address
rubrics_metrics.description: Honorific titles and respectful forms of address are capitalized in any context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Honorable Angus Stanley King Jr.; the Right Honourable Justin Trudeau; Her (His, Your) Majesty; Mr. President; Madam Speaker; Your Honor.' See 'Forms of Address' for comprehensive listings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epithets and bynames
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive or characterizing words or phrases used as part of or instead of a person’s name are capitalized; an initial 'the' that is part of such a name is not capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Great Emancipator (Abraham Lincoln); the Sun King (Louis XIV); the Wizard of Menlo Park (Thomas Edison).' When used in addition to a name, the epithet is enclosed in quotation marks: 'George Herman "Babe" Ruth.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Epithets as character names in drama/fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: In drama or fiction, epithets or generic titles used in place of names are normally capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'John Barrymore performed brilliantly as Chief Executioner. Alice encounters the Red Queen and the Mad Hatter.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinship names
rubrics_metrics.description: Kinship names are lowercased unless they immediately precede a personal name or are used alone in place of a personal name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'my father and mother; the Bronté sisters; Let’s write to Aunt Maud; She adores her aunt Maud.' Kinship terms used with religious offices follow similar rules: 'Brother Thomas.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Personifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Personifications (capitalizing abstractions as persons) are rare and are best confined to quoted material; normally do not capitalize abstractions used metaphorically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example quoted usage given; contrasted with normal lowercasing: 'In springtime, nature is at its best.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnic and national groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of ethnic and national groups and associated adjectives are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Aboriginal peoples; African Americans; American Indians; Arabs; Asians; the British; Caucasians; Chicanos; European Americans; French Canadians; Hispanics; Inuit; Italian Americans; Jews; Latinos; Métis; Native Americans; New Zealanders; Pygmies; Romanies.' Note terms such as 'black' and 'white' referring to ethnicity are usually lowercased unless an author/publisher prefers capitalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound nationalities (hyphenation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The hyphen in compound nationality terms (e.g., African American) may be omitted because the hyphen does not aid comprehension; author or publisher preference may control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chicago prefers omitting the hyphen unless a particular author or publisher prefers it. See related tables for geography/nationality entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms denoting socioeconomic classes or groups are lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the middle class; a middle-class neighborhood; the upper-middle class; an upper-middle-class family; the 1 percent; blue-collar workers; the aristocracy; the proletariat; homeless people.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual orientation and gender identity terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms referring to sexual orientation or gender identity/expression are lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'lesbians; lesbian history; gay men; transgender women; transgender men.' See guidance on pronoun use for individuals who do not identify with a gender-specific pronoun (5.48).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generation terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms denoting generations are usually lowercased, but lettered Generations X, Y, and Z are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the me generation; baby boomer(s); boomers; the MTV generation; the millennials; Generation X, Generation Y, Generation Z.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical characteristics and disability terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms describing groups by physical characteristics or disability are usually lowercased, with cultural-group exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'wheelchair users; blind persons; deaf children.' Note that 'Deaf' may be capitalized when referring to members of the distinct ASL-using cultural community; lowercase when referring to hearing loss or preference for oral methods. See 11.125.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place-name authoritative sources
rubrics_metrics.description: For spelling of place-names, consult authoritative geographical listings and prefer frequently updated online resources for modern place-names; use forms appropriate to historical periods in historical works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested resources: Merriam-Webster’s Collegiate Dictionary, Encyclopaedia Britannica, United States Board on Geographic Names, CIA World Factbook. For historical works, attempt to use period-appropriate forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of continents, countries, cities, oceans
rubrics_metrics.description: Entities that appear on maps—continents, countries, cities, oceans—are always capitalized, as are adjectives and nouns derived from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Asia; Asian; Ireland; Irish; California; Californian; Chicago; Chicagoan; Atlantic Ocean; Atlantic.' Note: initial 'the' as part of a name is lowercased in running text except rare cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Points of the compass
rubrics_metrics.description: Compass points and related terms are lowercased if they simply indicate direction or location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'pointing toward the north; a north wind; a northern climate; to fly east; an eastward move; in the southwest of France.' (See separate rules for region names where capitalization may differ.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Regions and national regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms that denote regions of the world or of a country are often capitalized, but usage varies with context and historical/political meaning; consult references and respect an author’s strong preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/notes: 'the Swiss Alps; the Australian Alps; the Alps; Alpine skiing (but alpine pastures in the Rockies); Central Europe vs central Europe depending on context (e.g., political division of WW I); the East, the Far East, Middle East; Eastern Hemisphere; eastern Europe (but Eastern Europe when referring to the post–World War II division). Consult Webster’s or an encyclopedia for ambiguous terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular place-names and epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular or colloquial place-names/epithets are usually capitalized and do not require quotation marks; avoid using names that will not be readily understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Back Bay; Silicon Valley; the Badger State; the Fertile Crescent; the Beltway; the Bible Belt; the Left Bank; the Village.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Political terms vs geographical capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain terms considered political rather than geographical need not be capitalized; editorial discretion advised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the iron curtain or Iron Curtain; the third world or Third World.' Context may justify capitalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban-area generic terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic terms for parts of urban areas are not capitalized; official administrative names may be capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the business district; the inner city; the metropolitan area; the greater Chicago metropolitan area; Chicagoland; the tristate area.' But 'Greater London' (official administrative region) is capitalized; local established usage may be favored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real versus metaphorical names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize proper-place names when referring to the real place; lowercase when used metaphorically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Stratford-upon-Avon is a mecca for Shakespeare enthusiasts.' (Mecca capitalized as proper place) vs 'She is trying to create a utopia for her children.' (utopia lowercased when metaphorical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political-division capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Words denoting political divisions (empire, republic, state, ward, precinct) are capitalized when they follow a name and are part of the accepted name; when preceding a name they are usually capitalized in country names but lowercased below national level; used alone they are usually lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Ottoman Empire; the empire; the United States; the republic; the Fifth Republic (France); the province of Ontario; Lake County; the county of Lake; the county.' Exceptions based on regional/historical context should be respected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governmental entities (full names)
rubrics_metrics.description: When referring to a specific governmental body rather than the place, words such as State or City are usually capitalized when part of the official name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'She works for the Village of Forest Park.' vs 'Residents of the village of Forest Park enjoy easy access to the city of Chicago.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Topographical feature names
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of mountains, rivers, oceans, islands, etc., are capitalized; the generic term is also capitalized when part of the name; pluralization rules depend on whether the generic is part of a single name or two/more names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Walden Pond; Silver Lake; Lake Michigan; Lakes Michigan and Erie; the Illinois River; the Nile River valley; the Great Barrier Reef; Mount Washington; Mounts Washington and Rainier; the Rocky Mountains; the Rockies.' See rules for valley/delta usage where the river forms part of the proper names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic geographic terms used descriptively
rubrics_metrics.description: When a generic geographic term is used descriptively (or in apposition) rather than as part of a name, or when used alone, it is lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Amazon basin; along the Pacific coast (but the West Coast); the California desert; the river Thames (descriptive usage).' Use dictionary/authority when unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-English geographic generic terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When a generic term from a language other than English forms part of a geographic name, do not add the English equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Rio Grande (not the Rio Grande River); Fujiyama (not Mount Fujiyama); Mauna Loa (not Mount Mauna Loa); the Sierra Nevada (not the Sierra Nevada Mountains).'

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of thoroughfares and public places
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of streets, avenues, squares, parks, and similar thoroughfares are capitalized; the generic term is lowercased when used alone but capitalized when part of a plural name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Broadway; Fifty-Fifth Street; Hyde Park Boulevard; the boulevard; Interstate 80; I-80; an interstate highway; the interstate; Jackson Park; the Mall (in London); Park Lane.' See also related sections on routes and numbered roads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buildings and monuments
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of buildings and monuments are generally capitalized; the generic term is usually lowercased when used alone but capitalized when part of a plural name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Berlin Wall; Buckingham Fountain; the Capitol; the Chrysler Building; the Houses of Parliament; the Jefferson Memorial; the Leaning Tower of Pisa; the Pyramids (but the Egyptian pyramids); the Statue of Liberty; Mount Rushmore National Memorial.' Note: some massive works of sculpture are regarded primarily as monuments and therefore not italicized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official room and office names
rubrics_metrics.description: Official names of rooms, offices, suites, and similar are capitalized; generic room numbers or generic references are lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Empire Room (but room 421); the Amelia Earhart Suite (but suite 219); the Lincoln Bedroom; the Oval Office; the West Wing of the White House.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-English names for places and structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-English names of thoroughfares and buildings are not italicized and may be preceded by English 'the' if the definite article appears in the original language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Champs-Elysées; Unter den Linden (never preceded by the); the Bibliotheque nationale; the Piazza delle Terme.' See 11.4 for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives derived from personal names
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives derived from personal names are normally capitalized; common forms may be found in dictionaries; if not, form with -ian/-an/-esque where suitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Baudelaire; Baudelairean; Bayes; Bayesian; Dickens; Dickensian; Foucault; Foucauldian; Kafka; Kafkaesque; Marx; Marxist; Mendel; Mendelian.' If a name does not lend itself to a coinage, avoid inventing a form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lowercasing words derived from proper names (nonliteral use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal, national, or geographical names and words derived from such names are often lowercased when used with a nonliteral meaning; Chicago prefers lowercase in many such nonliteral uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'anglicize; arabic numerals; burgundy; champagne; cheddar; french fries; roman numerals; swiss cheese (not made in Switzerland); scotch vs Scotch whisky (product of Scotland).' See 8.79 for related exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative and deliberative bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Full names of legislative and deliberative bodies, departments, bureaus, and offices are capitalized; adjectives derived from them are usually lowercased and many generic names used alone are lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the United Nations General Assembly; the UN General Assembly; the assembly; the United States Congress; the US Congress; the 115th Congress; Congress; the United States Senate; the Senate; senatorial; the House of Representatives; the House; the Electoral College; the Committee on Foreign Affairs; the Foreign Affairs Committee; the Chicago City Council; the city council.' For generic names not listed, opt for lowercase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Full names of administrative bodies are capitalized; adjectives derived from them are usually lowercased and many generic names used alone are lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the United States Census Bureau; census forms; the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; the CDC; the Department of the Interior; the Interior; the Department of State; the State Department; the department; departmental; the Federal Bureau of Investigation; the bureau; the FBI; the National Institutes of Health; the NIH.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: The full name of a court is capitalized (often including a place-name); subsequent references to a court are lowercased except for the phrase 'Supreme Court' at the national level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the United States Supreme Court; the Supreme Court; the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit; the court of appeals; the District Court for the Southern District of New York; the district court; the Circuit Court of Lake County, Family Division (Illinois); family court.' States vary in court naming—use the full name first before using generic terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government-related generic terms that are lowercased
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain generic terms associated with governmental bodies are lowercased (e.g., 'administration', 'cabinet', 'city hall', 'civil service'), with contextual exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'administration; the Carter administration; brain trust; cabinet (but the Kitchen Cabinet in Jackson administration); city hall; civil service; court (a royal court); executive, legislative, or judicial branch; federal; the federal government; government; monarchy; state; parliament (lowercased)'. Respect regional usages (e.g., Parliament in UK).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political parties, organizations, movements (official names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Official names of national/international organizations, alliances, political movements, and parties are capitalized; words like party, union, movement are capitalized when part of the official name; terms for formal members/adherents are usually capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the African National Congress; the ANC; Arab Socialist Ba‘th Party; the Communist Party; the Democratic Party; the Green Party; the Republican Party; the World Health Organization; WHO.' By contrast, names for systems of thought and references to adherents are often lowercased ('communism', 'communist'), though capitalization may be used consistently within a work to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherents of unofficial political groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Names for adherents of unofficial political groups and movements are usually lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'anarchist(s); centrist(s); independent(s); moderate(s); mugwump(s).' Exceptions: 'the Left; the Right; the Opposition' in specific British/Canadian contexts or when referring to established groupings.
